Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 15:

﴿O you who have believed, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing [in ranks]﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, "state") referring back to ﴿those who disbelieve﴾. Al-zaḥf (the advancing host) is the army which is seen, because of its large number, as if it is creeping (yazḥif), i.e., moving forward slowly step by step, from the zaḥf of a child, when it crawls on its buttocks a little at a time. It is named by the verbal noun (maṣdar) [in the sense of the participle]. ﴿Then do not turn your backs to them﴾: do not turn away from them in defeat. That is, when you meet them for battle, while they are many and you are few, do not flee, let alone bring yourselves close to them in number, or equal them. Alternatively, it is a ḥāl referring to the believers, or to both parties, meaning: when you meet them while you and they are advancing toward one another.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 16:

﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, unless he is swerving (mutaharrifan) for [the purpose of] battle,﴾ meaning inclining, ﴿for battle﴾ and this is the al-karr ba'da al-farr (the charge after the feigned retreat), by which he makes his enemy imagine that he is routed, then he turns back upon him, and this is one of the stratagems of war (khud'a al-harb).

﴿Or withdrawing (mutahayyizan) to a company﴾ joining himself ﴿to a company﴾ to a group of the Muslims other than the company in which he is, and these two are circumstantial clauses (hal) from the subject pronoun in "yuwalli-himm" (turns to them). ﴿Then he has incurred anger from Allah, and his abode is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ The measure (wazn) of mutahayyiz is mutafay'il, not mutaf'il, because the root is from "ḥāza, yaḥūzu" (to gain possession), so the form of mutaf'il from it would be mutaḥawwiz.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 17:

When they overcame the people of Makkah, killing and taking captives, and the killer among them would say boastfully, "I killed and I took captives," it was said to them: ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them.﴾ The fa' (fa, "so") is the answer to an implied condition, its sense being: "If you boast of killing them, then you did not kill them, ﴿but it was Allah who killed them.﴾" When Jibril (Gabriel) said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Take a handful of dust and throw it at them," he threw it into their faces and said, "May the faces be disfigured," and no polytheist remained except that he was occupied with his own eyes, and they fled. It was said: ﴿And you did not throw, O Muhammad, when you threw, but it was Allah who threw.﴾ This means: the throw you threw, you did not throw in the true sense, for if you had thrown it, its effect would not have reached beyond what the effect of a human throw reaches; rather, it was the throw of Allah, in that it produced that great effect. In the verse there is an indication that the act of the servant is attributed to him as acquisition (kasb), and to Allah Most High as creation (khalq), not as the Jabriyyah (Determinists) and the Mu'tazilah say, because He affirmed the act from the servant by His saying ﴿when you threw﴾, then negated it from him and affirmed it for Allah Most High by His saying ﴿but it was Allah who threw.﴾ ﴿But it was Allah who killed them.﴾ (Wa-lakinna Allaha rama) with the lightening of (lakin) is read by Ibn 'Amir (al-Shami), Hamzah, and 'Ali.

﴿And that He might bestow upon the believers from Him a good favour⁠﴾, that He might give them from Himself a fine gift. The meaning: for the benefaction of the believers He did what He did, and He did not do it except for that.

﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing⁠﴾ of their supplication, ﴿All-Knowing⁠﴾ of their circumstances.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 18:

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the good trial (al-balaʾ al-hasan), and its place in the sentence is in the nominative case (rafʿ), meaning: what is intended is ﴿that﴾. ﴿And that Allah is weakening the scheme of the disbelievers﴾ is conjoined to "that" (dhalikum), meaning: what is intended is the trial of the believers and the weakening of the scheme of the disbelievers. (Muwahhin kayd) is read by al-Shami and by the Kufans other than Hafs. (Muwahhin kayd) is read by Hafs. (Muwahhin kayda) is read by the others.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 19:

﴿If you seek a decision, then the decision has indeed come to you﴾: that is, if you seek victory, then victory has indeed come to you against you. This is an address to the people of Makkah, because when they wanted to set out (to fight), they clung to the curtains of the Ka'bah and said: "O Allah, if Muhammad is upon the truth, then support him, and if we are upon the truth, then support us." It has also been said that ﴿If you seek a decision﴾ is an address to the believers, and ﴿And if you desist﴾ is for the disbelievers.

﴿And if you desist﴾ from enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿then it﴾, i.e., the desisting, ﴿is better for you﴾ and more secure (aslam).

﴿And if you return﴾ to fighting him, ﴿We shall return﴾ to supporting him against you. ﴿And your company will avail you nothing, however numerous it may be﴾ in number. (And that Allah is with the believers): read with the fat-ḥa (وَأنَّ) by Madani, Shami and Ḥafs. That is: and because Allah is with the believers in victory, that was the case; and with the kasra (وَإنَّ) by the others. This is supported by the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): ﴿and Allah is with the believers﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 20:

﴿O you who believe, obey God and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him﴾ (from the Messenger of God ﷺ). This is because the meaning is: "And obey the Messenger of God," as in His saying: ﴿God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62]. And because obedience to the Messenger and obedience to God are one thing: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed God﴾ [al-Nisa: 80]. So the return of the pronoun (ḍamīr) to one of the two is like its return to both of them, as in your saying: "Kindness and generosity do not benefit so-and-so." Or the pronoun returns to the command to obey, meaning: "Do not turn away from this command and its like." Its original form is ولا تَتَوَلَّوْا (wa-lā tatawallaw), so one of the two tā' was dropped for lightening (takhfīf). ﴿And you hear﴾, meaning: and you hear it. Or, ﴿and do not turn away﴾ from the Messenger of God ﷺ, and do not oppose him, ﴿while you hear﴾, meaning: while you accept it as true, because you are believers, not like the deaf disbelievers who deny.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 21:

﴿And do not be like those who say, "We hear,"﴾ That is: they claimed to hear, and they are the hypocrites (munafiqun) and the People of the Book. ﴿while they do not hear.﴾ Because they are not believers in what they hear, so it is as if they were not hearers. The meaning is: you affirm the Qur'an and prophethood, so when you turn away from obeying the Messenger in some matters, such as the division of the spoils of war (ghana'im) and other things, your hearing resembles the hearing of one who does not believe. Then he said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 22:

﴿Indeed, the worst of creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the dumb who do not use their reason.﴾ That is: indeed, the worst of those that crawl upon the face of the earth are the beasts; and indeed, the worst of the beasts are those who are deaf to the truth and do not comprehend it. He made them of the kind of beasts, then He made them the worst of them, because they obstinately opposed after understanding, and defiantly persisted after reasoning.

(p-639)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 23:

﴿And if Allah had known any good in them﴾ in these deaf and dumb ones, ﴿good﴾ meaning sincerity and eagerness, ﴿He would have made them hear﴾ He would have made them listen, until they heard the hearing of those who affirm the truth. ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away﴾ from it. That is: even if He had made them hear, and they had been sincere, they would have apostatised after that and would not have remained upright.

﴿while they are turning away﴾ from belief.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 24:

﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life.﴾ He also made the pronoun singular, as he did in what came before, because responding to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is like responding to Allah. By "response" (istijabah) is meant obedience and compliance, and by "calling" (da'wah) is meant rousing and urging.

﴿That which gives you life﴾: this refers to the knowledge of the religions and the laws (shara'i'), because knowledge is life, just as ignorance is death. The poet said:

Do not be impressed by the ignorant man's finery, for he is dead, and his garment is a shroud.

Or it refers to fighting the disbelievers, because if they abandoned it, the disbelievers would overcome them and kill them. Or it refers to martyrdom, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿Nay, they are alive with their Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169].

﴿And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart﴾, that is, He causes him to die, so the opportunity he possesses slips away from him, and that opportunity is the ability to make the heart sincere. So seize this opportunity, and make your hearts sincere in obedience to Allah and His Messenger. Or [it means] He intervenes between him and what he wishes in his heart of long life, so He dissolves his resolutions.

﴿And that to Him you will be gathered﴾: know that you will be gathered to Him, and He will reward you according to the soundness of your hearts and the sincerity of your obedience.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 25:

﴿And beware of a trial﴾ (a punishment) ﴿which will not strike those of you who have done wrong in particular﴾. It is an answer to the imperative (jawab al-amr), meaning: if it strikes you, it will not strike only the wrongdoers among you in particular, but it will encompass you all. It is permissible for the emphatic nun (al-nun al-mu'akkidah) to enter the answer to an imperative, because it carries the sense of a prohibition (nahy), as when you say: "Get down from the animal, it will not throw you," and it is permissible to say: "it will not throw you" (with the emphatic nun added: la tatrahannaka). The "min" in "minkum" is for partition (li-l-tab'id). ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ when He punishes.

(p. 640)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 26:

﴿Remember when you were few and oppressed in the land﴾ is a direct object (maf'ul bihi) and not an adverb of time (zarf). That is: remember the time when you were few and humbled. ﴿Oppressed in the land﴾ refers to the land of Makkah before the Hijrah, where the Quraysh oppressed you. ﴿Fearing that the people would snatch you away﴾ because the people were hostile enemies to them. ﴿He sheltered you﴾ in Madinah. ﴿And strengthened you with His help﴾ through the support of the Ansar and through the reinforcement of the angels on the Day of Badr. ﴿And provided you with good things﴾ from the spoils of war, which had not been made lawful to anyone before you. ﴿That perhaps you would be grateful﴾ for these blessings.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 27:

﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah﴾ by failing to perform His obligations (farā'iḍahu), ﴿and the Messenger﴾ by not following his sunna (bi-allā tastannū bihi). ﴿And betray﴾ is jussive (jazm) as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on ﴿do not betray﴾, meaning: and do not betray ﴿your trusts﴾ among yourselves by not guarding them, ﴿while you know﴾ the consequence of that and its harm. Or ﴿while you know﴾ that you are betraying, meaning: betrayal occurs from you deliberately, not through forgetfulness. Or: while you are scholars (ʿulamāʾ, religious scholars) who know the goodness of good and the ugliness of ugly things.

The meaning of khawn (betrayal) is deficiency (naqṣ), just as the meaning of wafāʾ (fulfilment) is completeness (tamām). From it comes takhawwanahu, meaning he diminished him. Then it was used for the opposite of trustworthiness (amāna) and fidelity (wafāʾ), because when you betray a man in something, you have introduced deficiency into it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 28:

﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ i.e., they are a cause of falling into trial (fitna), which is sin and punishment; or they are a test from Allah, that He may try you to see how you guard the limits of His law concerning them. ﴿And that with Allah there is a great reward.﴾ So it is incumbent upon you to be eager to seek that reward, to be detached from the world, and not to be greedy in gathering wealth or in loving children.

O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan) — victory, because He distinguishes between truth and disbelief by humbling the party of disbelief and by exalting Islam through honouring its people. Or (it means) clear proof and manifestation that makes your affair famous and spreads your renown and your traces throughout the lands of the earth, from their saying: "the furqan has shone forth," meaning: the dawn has risen. Or (it means) a way out of doubts and an expansion of the breasts. Or (it means) a distinction between you and others among the people of other religions, and grace and excellence in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And He will remove from you your misdeeds﴾, meaning the minor sins, ﴿and forgive you﴾, meaning your major sins. ﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ toward His servants.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 30:

﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ When Allah granted him victory over them, He reminded him of the plot of the Quraysh against him while he was in Makkah, so that he would give thanks for the blessing of Allah in his deliverance from their scheming and his triumph over them. The meaning is: "Remember when they were plotting against you." This occurred because when the Ansar embraced Islam, the Quraysh feared that his affair would grow greatly, so they gathered in Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of the Quraysh) to consult about his matter. Iblis entered upon them in the form of an old man and said: "I am an elder from Najd. I entered Makkah and heard of your gathering, so I wished to attend, and you will not lack from me an opinion and counsel." Abu al-Bukhturi said: "My opinion is that you imprison him in a house, bind his shackles, and seal its door except for a small opening through which you pass him his food and drink, and wait for him to meet the fate of mortals." Iblis said: "What a bad opinion! His people will come to fight you and rescue him from your hands." Hisham ibn 'Amr said: "My opinion is that you load him on a camel and expel him from amongst you; then his deeds will not harm you, and you will be relieved of him." Iblis said: "What a bad opinion! He will corrupt another people and fight you with them." Abu Jahl—may Allah curse him—said: "I see that you should take a young man from every clan and give each a sword, and they should strike him with one blow as a single man, so his blood will be spread among the tribes, and the Banu Hashim will not be able to fight all of the Quraysh. When they demand the blood-money, we will pay it and be relieved." The accursed one said: "This young man has spoken the truth; he is the best of you in opinion." So they dispersed, agreeing upon the opinion of Abu Jahl, united in killing him. Jibril (peace be upon him) informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and commanded him not to sleep in his bed, and Allah permitted him to emigrate. He commanded 'Ali, so he slept in his bed and said to him: "Wrap yourself in my cloak, for no harm you dislike will reach you." They spent the night watching, and when they awoke they rushed to his bed (p-642) and saw 'Ali, and they were dumbfounded, and Allah frustrated their effort, and they followed his trail, but Allah nullified their plot.

﴿to imprison you﴾ to confine you and bind you; ﴿or kill you﴾ with their swords; ﴿or expel you﴾ from Makkah. ﴿And they plot﴾ they conceal their schemes against him. ﴿And Allah plots﴾ Allah conceals what He has prepared for them until it comes upon them suddenly. ﴿And Allah is the best of planners﴾ meaning: His plotting is more effective than the plotting of others, and more far-reaching in its effect.

The Prophet (ﷺ) would recite the Qur'an and, in his recitation, mention the accounts of earlier generations. Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: "If I wished, I could say something like this. He (Muhammad) came from the lands of Persia with a copy of the story of Rustam and the tales of the non-Arabs." So the following was revealed: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾, i.e., the Qur'an,

﴿they say: "We have heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾ This is arrogance and impudence on his part, because they were challenged to produce a single surah like this Qur'an, and they did not produce it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 32:

﴿And when they said: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You"﴾ That is, the Qur'an. "Hadha" is the subject (ism) of kāna (is), "huwa" is a separator (fasl, a particle that marks a definite predicate), and "al-haqq" is the predicate (khabar) of kāna. It is narrated that when al-Nadr said, "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients," the Prophet ﷺ said to him, "Woe to you, this is the speech of Allah." Al-Nadr raised his head toward the sky and said: ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾. That is: if the Qur'an is the truth, then punish us for denying it with sijjil (baked clay stones), as You did to the people of the Elephant, ﴿or bring us a painful punishment﴾ of another kind from the category of painful punishment. He was killed on the Day of Badr by being bound and executed (ṣabran).

It is also related from Mu'awiya that he said to a man from Saba': "How ignorant your people are, that they made a woman their ruler." The man said: "Your people are more ignorant than mine. They said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he invited them to the truth: ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ and they did not say: 'If this is indeed the truth, then guide us to it.'"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 33:

﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them.﴾ The lam (the lam of emphasis) is for emphasizing the negation, and it indicates that punishing them while you are among them is not proper, because you were sent as a mercy to the worlds. His custom (sunnah) is not to punish a people with a punishment of extermination (isti'sal) as long as their Prophet is among them. It also implies that they are awaiting punishment should he emigrate from them. ﴿And Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness.﴾ This is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and its meaning is the negation of seeking forgiveness from them, i.e., even if they were among those who believe and seek forgiveness from disbelief, He would not have punished them. Or its meaning is: Allah would not punish them while among them are those who seek forgiveness, namely the Muslims among them, from among the weak ones who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 34:

﴿And what is it with them that Allah should not punish them﴾ That is: Allah would not punish them while you (O Muhammad) are among them, and He is (still) going to punish them once you have departed from them. And what is it with them that Allah should not punish them,

﴿while they bar (people) from the Sacred Mosque﴾ And how could they not be punished, when their condition is that they bar (people) from the Sacred Mosque, just as they barred the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. And their expelling the Messenger of Allah and the believers from (the Sacred Mosque) was (a form of) barring. They used to say: "We are the guardians of the House and the Sacred Precinct, so we bar whom we will and admit whom we will." Then it was said: ﴿And they were not its guardians﴾, meaning: they did not deserve, given their polytheism and their enmity towards the religion, to be the custodians of the affairs of the Sacred Precinct. ﴿Its guardians are only the God-fearing﴾ among the Muslims. It has also been said: the two pronouns refer back to Allah,

﴿but most of them do not know﴾ this. It is as if (Allah) made an exception for those who knew (the truth) but were obstinate. Or He meant by "most" the whole, just as "few" is sometimes used to mean "none."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 35:

﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping.﴾ "Whistling" (mukā') is a sound like the call of the mukā', a bird of pleasant voice. It is on the pattern fu'āl, from makā yamkū, meaning to whistle. "Clapping" (tasdiyah) means handclapping, a form taf'ilah from al-ṣadā (echo). The reason is that they used to circumambulate the House naked, interlacing their fingers, whistling through them and clapping. They would do something similar whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in his prayer, confusing him.

﴿So taste the punishment﴾: the punishment of killing and captivity on the day of Badr,

﴿for what you used to disbelieve﴾: because of your disbelief.

Al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil (Commentary on Surah 8, verse 36):

It was revealed concerning the ones who fed (al-mut'imin) on the Day of Badr. They were twelve men, all of them from Quraysh, and each of them used to feed (people) ten camels every day. "Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to averted (others) from the way of Allah." That is: their purpose in spending was to turn people away from following Muhammad ﷺ, and he is the way of Allah. "So they will spend it, then it will be a regret for them." Then the consequence of their spending it will be remorse and regret, as if its very substance will become remorse and will turn into regret. "Then they will be overcome" in the end. This is one of the proofs of prophethood, because he (ﷺ) informed of it before it occurred, and it happened just as he had informed. "And those who disbelieve" — and the disbelievers among them — "to Hell they will be gathered." (This is stated) because among them there were some who embraced Islam and whose Islam was sound.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 37:

The lam in ﴿That Allah may distinguish the wicked﴾, namely the wicked group among the disbelievers, ﴿from the good﴾, i.e., from the good group among the believers, is connected to "yuhsharun" (they will be gathered). (Liyumayyiza) is read by Hamza and Ali. ﴿And place the wicked﴾, the wicked group, ﴿one upon another, and heap it all together﴾, i.e., gather it, ﴿and put it in Hell﴾, i.e., the wicked group.

﴿Those are the losers﴾: i.e., "those" is a reference to the wicked group, ﴿who are the losers﴾ of their own souls and their wealth.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 38:

﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾, that is, Abu Sufyan and his companions, ﴿if they desist﴾ from what they are upon of enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and fighting him, by entering into Islam, ﴿their past will be forgiven﴾ for them, of enmity; ﴿but if they return﴾ to fighting him, ﴿then the way of the former peoples has already passed﴾, namely destruction in this world and punishment in the Hereafter.

(p-645) Or its meaning is: when the disbelievers desist from disbelief and embrace Islam, what has passed of disbelief and sins is forgiven for them. And Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) took this as evidence for the view that an apostate who embraces Islam is not obliged to make up the acts of worship he neglected.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 39:

﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾ — until there is no longer any shirk found among them at all. ﴿And [until] the religion is entirely for Allah﴾ — every false religion vanishes from them, and only the religion of Islam remains among them alone. ﴿But if they desist﴾ from disbelief and embrace Islam, ﴿then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾ — He will reward them for their Islam.

And if they turn away (﻿وَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا), i.e., they turn away from faith and do not desist, ﴿then know that Allah is your Protector (مَوْلاكُمْ)﴾, your Helper and your Supporter. So trust in His guardianship and His support. ﴿How excellent a Protector!﴾ He does not abandon whoever takes Him as protector, ﴿and how excellent a Helper!﴾ He is not overcome whoever He helps. The one specified for praise is omitted.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 41:

﴿And know that whatever you gain [of spoils]﴾. "Ma" is in the sense of "alladhi" (that which). It may only be written separately; for if it were written joined, then "ma" would have to be a kafffa (the particle that restricts the governing word, "ma" as a restrictive particle). "Ghanimtum" is its relative clause (silah), and the returning pronoun (ha'id) is omitted; the implied sense is: "alladhi ghanimtumuhu" (that which you gained), ﴿from anything﴾ is its explanation (bayan). It has been said: even a thread or a needle.

﴿then to Allah belongs one-fifth of it﴾. The fa' (then) entered because "alladhi" carries the meaning of conditional (mujazah). "Anna" and what it governs are in a position of nominative (raf') as the predicate (khabar) of an implied subject (mubtada'), its estimate being: "fa-al-hukm: anna li-Allahi khumusahu" (so the ruling is: that one-fifth of it belongs to Allah).

﴿and to the Messenger, and to the near kin, and the orphans, and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾. In the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the khums was divided into five shares: one share for the Messenger of Allah, one share for his close relatives from the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, to the exclusion of the Banu 'Abd Shams and the Banu Nawfal (they were entitled to it at that time by virtue of support, due to the incident of 'Uthman and Jubayr ibn Mut'im), and three shares for the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer. As for after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his share lapses upon his death, and likewise the share of the near kin; they are given only because of their poverty, and their wealthy are not given. It is then distributed among the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was (p-646) divided into six: for Allah and the Messenger, two shares, and one share for his relatives until he passed away. Then Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, distributed the khums among three, and so did 'Umar and those after him among the caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them all. The meaning of "for Allah and for the Messenger" is: for the Messenger of Allah, like His saying: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62].

﴿If you have believed in Allah﴾: then act upon it, and be content with this division, for faith necessitates contentment with the ruling and acting upon knowledge.

﴿and what We sent down﴾ is conjoined to "in Allah", meaning: ﴿If you have believed in Allah﴾ and in what was sent down ﴿upon Our servant on the Day of Criterion﴾, the Day of Badr, ﴿the day the two hosts met﴾, the two groups of the Muslims and the disbelievers. The intended meaning is: what was sent down to him of the signs, the angels, and the victory on that day. It is a substitution (badal) for "the Day of Criterion".

﴿And Allah is over all things Powerful﴾, able to grant victory to the few over the many, as He did with you on the Day of Badr.

**[Surah al-Anfal, verse 42]**

﴿When you were﴾: *idh antum* is in apposition (*badal*) to *yawma al-furqan* ("the Day of Criterion"). Alternatively, the implied sense is: "Remember when you were..."

﴿on the near side﴾ (*al-'udwa*) meaning the bank (*shatt*) of the valley. Makki and Abu 'Amr read both *bi-l-'udwa* and *al-dunya* with a kasra (*bi-l-kasr*). *Al-dunya* means the nearer side, toward Madinah, the feminine of *al-adna* (nearer). ﴿And they were on the far side﴾ means the farther side from Madinah, the feminine of *al-aqsa* (farthest). Both *kilta* forms are *fu'la* forms from roots with *waw*. Regular analogy would convert the *waw* to *ya'*, as in *al-'ulya*, the feminine of *al-a'la* (highest). *Al-quswa*, however, retains the original *waw*, like *al-qawd* in its form.

﴿And the caravan﴾ (*al-rakb*) means the merchant caravan (*al-'ir*). It is a plural in meaning of *rakib* (rider).

﴿Below you﴾ (*asfala minkum*) is in the accusative as an adverb of place (*zarf*), meaning a place lower than your place. That is, it was at the bottom of the valley, three miles away. Its position in the sentence is in the nominative (*marfu' al-mahall*), because it is the predicate (*khabar*) of the subject (*mubtada'*).

﴿Even if you had made an appointment﴾, you and the people of Makkah, and had agreed among yourselves upon a meeting place where you would meet for battle, ﴿you would have differed about the appointment﴾. That is, some of you would have opposed others. The fewness of your numbers and the greater number of the enemy would have prevented you from keeping the appointment, and what was in their hearts of awe of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims would have held them back as well. Thus you would not have achieved the meeting that Allah granted, and which He caused to happen. But ("wa-lakin") He gathered you together without an appointment ﴿so that Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾, namely the strengthening of His religion and the elevation of His word. The *lam* (of purpose) is connected to an omitted element, meaning: so that Allah might accomplish a matter that ought to be done, which is the victory of His allies and the subjugation of His enemies. He arranged that.

Shaykh Abu Mansur, may Allah have mercy on him, said: *al-qada'* (decree/accomplishment) may carry the sense of judgment, meaning: that He might judge what He knew would certainly happen; or that He might complete a matter that He had willed. Whatever He wills to occur is necessarily done. This matter is the honour of Islam and its people, and the humiliation of unbelief and its party. It is connected to *yaqdi* (accomplish).

﴿That whoever perished might perish upon clear proof, and whoever lived might live upon clear proof﴾. *Hayiya* (with the ya' as the second radical) is read by Nafi' and Abu 'Amr. The assimilation (*idgham*) is due to the meeting of two identical letters (*iltiqa' al-mithlayn*), while the non-assimilated reading is because the vowel of the second is not fixed, since in the future tense one says *yahya*. Assimilation is more common.

Destruction and life are used metaphorically for unbelief and faith. That is, the unbelief of whoever disbelieved would come about upon clear evidence, not from the intrusion of doubt, so that he would have no argument against Allah. Likewise, the Islam of whoever embraced Islam would come about through certainty and knowledge that it is the religion of truth, which must be entered and held fast to. The battle of Badr was among the clear signs, such that whoever disbelieved after it was stubbornly opposing his own self and deceiving himself. For this reason, the verse mentions the positions of the two groups, and that the caravan was below them, even though they had all seen this themselves. This is so that people would know that victory and dominance are not achieved through numbers and means, but through Allah the Exalted.

That is because the far side, where the polytheists had camped, had water and was a land without difficulty. The near side had no water and was soft ground (*khabar*) in which feet sink, and one could walk there only with exhaustion and hardship. The caravan was behind the backs of the enemy, despite the enemy's great numbers and equipment and the small number and weakness of the Muslims. Then what happened, happened.

﴿And indeed Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of their words, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the unbelief of whoever disbelieved and his punishment, and of the faith of whoever believed and his reward.

﴿When Allah showed them to you﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, اذْكُرْ (udhkur, "remember"), or it is connected to His saying: (p-٦٤٨) ﴿Indeed He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, meaning: He knows the interests (of the matter) when He makes them seem few to you ﴿in your sleep, few﴾, meaning: in your dream. This is because Allah Most High showed them to him in his dream as few, and he informed his companions of that, and that was an encouragement to them against their enemy. ﴿And if He had shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart﴾: you would have become cowardly and shrunk from advancing. ﴿And you would have disputed about the matter﴾, the matter of fighting, and vacillated between standing firm and fleeing. ﴿But Allah saved [you]﴾: He protected, and bestowed safety from failure, dispute and disagreement.

﴿Indeed He knows what is in the breasts﴾: He knows what will be in them of boldness, cowardice, patience and impatience.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 44:

﴿And when He shows them to you, [O Muhammad], as few when you met, and He makes you appear few in their eyes﴾ The two pronouns (al-damiran) are objects (maf'ulan), meaning: He makes you see them (yubassiru-kum iyyahum). ﴿When you met﴾ at the time of the encounter. ﴿In your eyes, few﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). He made them appear few in their eyes only to confirm the dream of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and so that they would witness what he had told them, whereby their certainty would increase, they would strive, and they would stand firm. Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "They were made to appear few in our eyes, to the extent that I said to a man beside me: 'Do you think they are seventy?' He said: 'I think they are a hundred,' and they were a thousand." ﴿And He makes you appear few in their eyes﴾, to the extent that one of them said: "They are only a mouthful of camel meat." It is said: He made them appear few in your eyes before the encounter, then made them appear many in your eyes after it, so that you would be bold against them, out of indifference toward them, then the multitude would suddenly strike them, and they would be stunned and fear. It is also permissible that they were made to see the many as few, by Allah covering some of them with a veil, or by creating in their eyes something that makes them consider the many to be little, as was done to the eyes of the squint-eyed, who see one as two. It was said to one of them: "The squint-eyed sees one as two," and he had one rooster before him, so he said: "What is wrong with me, that I do not see these two roosters as four?!" ﴿That Allah may accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾, and ﴿to Allah all matters are returned﴾, so that He judges concerning them as He wills. (Tur'aju) is the reading of al-Shami, Hamzah, and Ali.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 45:

﴿O you who have believed, when you meet a company (fi'ah) [of disbelievers in battle]﴾ — i.e., when you fight a group of the disbelievers. He omitted describing it, because the believers did not meet anyone except disbelievers. And "liqa'" (meeting) is a term dominantly used for fighting.

﴿Then stand firm﴾ for their fighting, and do not flee.

﴿And remember Allah much﴾ in the places of war, seeking support through His remembrance, seeking victory through Him, and invoking Him against your enemy: "O Allah, forsake them! O Allah, cut off their root!"

﴿That you may be successful﴾ — that you may attain your desire, of victory and reward. In it is an indication that the servant should not slacken in the remembrance of his Lord, at the time when his heart is most preoccupied and his concern is greatest, and that his soul should be gathered to that remembrance even if it is scattered away from everything else.

Obey Allah and His Messenger in the matter of fighting and steadfastness against the enemy, and other matters, ﴿and do not dispute, lest you lose heart﴾, that is, become cowardly. It is in the subjunctive by the implied "an" (that), and what indicates it is: ﴿and your strength depart﴾, that is, your dynasty (dawla). It is said: "The winds of so-and-so have blown," when fortune has favored him and his command has taken effect. The strength (rih) was likened, in the taking effect of its command and its going forth, to the wind (rih) and its blowing. It was also said: victory never came except by a wind that Allah sends. And in a hadith: "I was made victorious by the east wind (al-saba), and 'Ad were destroyed by the west wind (al-dabur)." ﴿And be patient﴾ in fighting the enemy and in other things, ﴿indeed Allah is with the patient﴾, that is, their helper and their protector.

﴿And do not be like those who went forth from their homes insolently and to be seen by people.﴾ They are the people of Makkah when they set out out of zeal for the caravan (ḥamiyyat al-ʿīr). Then Abu Sufyan's messenger came to them, saying: "Turn back, for your caravan has been saved." But Abu Jahl refused and said: "Not until we reach Badr, and drink wine there, slaughter camels, have singing girls (qiyān) play for us, and feed the Arabs with it." That was their insolence (baṭar). Their showing off to the people (riyāʾuhum al-nās) was by feeding them. So they arrived there, and they were given the cups of death instead of wine, and the mourning women wailed over them in place of the singing girls. Thus He forbade them from being like them, insolent, exultant, and showing off with their deeds, and commanded them to be among the people of piety, sorrow and grief out of fear of God, (p-650) sincerely dedicating their deeds to God. Baṭar is that abundance of blessing preoccupies one from giving thanks for it.

﴿And they bar from the way of God﴾, the religion of God, ﴿and God is encompassing of what they do﴾, knowing, and this is a warning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 48:

﴿And when Satan made their deeds seem attractive to them and said, "No one among the people can overcome you today, and I am a protector for you."﴾ And mention, "when Satan made their deeds seem attractive to them," the deeds they had done in opposing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he whispered to them that they could not be overcome. The word "ghalib" (no overcomer) is indeclinable (mabni), like in "la rajul" (there is no man). "Lakum" (for you) is in the place of nominative case as the predicate (khabar) of "la" (there is no), its implied meaning being: "No overcomer exists for you."

﴿And I am a protector for you﴾, i.e., one who gives protection to you. He made them imagine that obeying Satan would protect them. ﴿So when the two hosts saw each other﴾, i.e., when the two groups met, ﴿he turned back on his heels﴾ — Satan fled, ﴿on his heels﴾, i.e., he retreated backward, ﴿and said, "Indeed I am free of you"﴾, i.e., "I have withdrawn from the security I guaranteed to you." It is narrated that Iblis appeared to them in the form of Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum, with a host of devils, and with him a banner. When he saw the angels descending, he turned back. Al-Harith ibn Hisham said to him, "Will you abandon us in this situation?" He said, ﴿"Indeed I see what you do not see"﴾, i.e., the angels. And they were routed. When they reached Mecca they said, "Suraqah has defeated the people." This reached Suraqah, and he said, "By Allah, I did not know of your march until your defeat reached me." When they embraced Islam, they realized that it had been Satan. ﴿"Indeed I fear Allah"﴾, i.e., His punishment, ﴿and Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

Remember when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said, in Medina, "Their religion has deluded these people." This is a description of the hypocrites. Or it is intended: "those who are on an edge" (ʿalā ḥarf), who are not firm-footed in Islam.

"Their religion has deluded these people." They mean: the Muslims were deluded by their religion, so they went out, three hundred and some ten (ten and a few), against about a thousand. Then He said, as a reply to them: "And whoever puts his trust in Allah" (yakil ilayhi amrahu), i.e., entrusts his affair to Him, "then indeed Allah is Mighty" (ʿazīz), overpowering, who empowers the few and weak over the many and strong, "Wise" (ḥakīm), who does not treat His friend and His enemy alike.

(p-651)

﴿And if you could see﴾, that is, if you were to witness and observe it. "Law" (lau) turns the present-tense verb (muḍāriʿ) into the meaning of the past, just as "in" turns the past-tense verb (māḍī) into the meaning of the future. ﴿When﴾: "idh" is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf). ﴿The angels take the souls of those who disbelieved﴾, by seizing their spirits. ﴿The angels﴾ is the subject (fāʿil). ﴿Striking﴾ (yaḍribūna) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, "circumstantial accusative") referring to them. ﴿Their faces﴾, when they turn toward them, ﴿and their backs﴾, their backs and buttocks when they turn away. Or: their faces at the moment of advancing, and their backs at the moment of fleeing. It has also been said that in "yatawaffā" the pronoun refers to God, Exalted is He, that "al-malāʾikatu" is a nominative subject (mubtadaʾ), and that "yaḍribūna" is its predicate (khabar). The first view is the preferred one, because the disbelievers do not deserve that God, Exalted is He, should take their souls directly without an intermediary. Its evidence is the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir, "tatawaffā" with a ta'. ﴿And taste﴾: and they say to them, "dhūqū" is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to "yaḍribūna".

﴿The torment of the burning﴾: that is, the foretaste of the torment of the Fire. Or: taste the torment of the Hereafter, as good news to them of it. Or it is said to them on the Day of Resurrection: taste. The response (jawāb) of "law" is omitted, meaning: you would see a dreadful matter.

That is due to what your hands have sent forward — i.e., what you earned (kasabat). This is a refutation of the Jabriyya (the determinist school), and it is either part of the speech of Allah Most High or part of the speech of the angels. "Dhalika" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "bi-ma qaddamat" is its predicate (khabar). "Wa-anna Allah" is conjoined to it (ma'tuf 'alayhi), meaning: that punishment is for two reasons: because of your disbelief and your sins, and because Allah is ﴿not unjust to the servants﴾, since punishing the disbelievers is part of justice. It has also been said that "zallam" (in the intensive form) is for emphasis regarding the servants, or to negate all kinds of injustice.

The kaf in ﴿kada'b ali Fir'awn﴾ is in the nominative position (maḥall al-raf'), meaning: the habit of these people is like the habit of the family of Pharaoh. Their da'b (habit) is their custom and their practice to which they were persistent, i.e., they kept to it constantly. ﴿Those who came before them﴾: before the Quraysh, or before the family of Pharaoh. ﴿Disbelieved﴾ is an explanation of the habit of the family of Pharaoh. ﴿In the signs of Allah, so Allah seized them for their sins. Indeed Allah is Strong, severe in punishment.﴾ The meaning: they proceeded according to their habit of denial, so Allah brought upon them the same as what He had done to them in punishment.

(p-652)

﴿That﴾ [i.e., the punishment, or the retribution], ﴿because Allah does not change a blessing He has bestowed upon a people until they change what is in themselves﴾. The meaning is: it is because Allah, in His wisdom, is not fitting to change His blessing upon a people until they change the state they are in. Yes, the Pharaoh's people (Āl Fir'awn) and the polytheists of Makkah did not previously have a pleasing state which they then changed into a displeasing one; rather, when the pleasing state changed into a displeasing one, the displeasing state changed into one even more displeasing. Those people, before the Messenger was sent to them, were disbelievers who worshipped idols. When he was sent to them with the signs and they denied him, and strove to shed his blood, they changed their state to one worse than what it had been. So Allah changed the favour He had bestowed upon them, namely the respite (al-imhal), and hastened punishment upon them. ﴿And that Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of what those who deny the messengers say, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of what they do.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 54:

﴿Like the case of the people of Pharaoh﴾ is a repetition for emphasis, or because in the first (verse) there was the seizing for sins without clarifying that this was destruction and uprooting, whereas here he clarified that this is destruction and uprooting. ﴿And those before them denied the signs of their Lord﴾. In His saying ﴿the signs of their Lord﴾ there is added indication of ungratefulness for blessings (kufran al-ni'am) and denial of the truth (juhud al-haqq).

﴿So We destroyed them for their sins and drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾ in the water of the sea. ﴿And all﴾ — all of them, from the drowned Copts and the slain of Quraysh.

﴿They were wrongdoers﴾ to themselves through disbelief and sins.

Verse 55 of Surah al-Anfal (8): "Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve, and they will not believe."

That is, they persisted in disbelief, so faith is not to be expected from them.

**﴿Those with whom you made a covenant among them﴾** is a substitution (badal) for "﴿those who disbelieved﴾." That is: those whom you made a covenant with from among those who disbelieved. And He made them "the worst of beasts," because the worst of people are the disbelievers, the worst of the disbelievers are the persistent ones (al-musirrun), and the worst of the persistent ones are those who break their covenants (al-nakithun li-l-'uhud).

**﴿Then they break their covenant every time﴾** in (p-653) every covenant **﴿and they do not fear (Allah)﴾**, meaning they do not fear the consequence of treachery, and they do not care about the shame and the Fire that it entails.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 57:

﴿Then if you gain the upper hand over them in war⦆ — that is, if you encounter them and get the better of them. ﴿then make an example of them to those behind them⦆ — that is, disperse those who are behind them from waging war against you and opposing you, by killing them in the most severe manner, and by inflicting such punishment upon them, among the disbelievers who are behind them, that none after them will dare to oppose you, taking heed from their example and being admonished by their condition. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian and Qur'an scholar) said: Do to them what disperses their gathering and drives away those other than them. ﴿So that they may take heed⦆ — so that those dispersed who are behind them may be admonished.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 58:

﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾ with whom you have a covenant, ﴿treachery﴾ meaning breach of the pact, through signs that become apparent to you, ﴿then throw back to them﴾ i.e., cast the covenant back to them ﴿on equal terms﴾, i.e., on a footing of equality between you and them in knowledge of the breaking of the covenant. This is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) relating to the one who throws back (al-nābidh) and to those to whom it is thrown back, meaning: you being on an equal footing in knowledge. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous﴾, those who break the covenants.

(59) (Wa-la yahsabanna): with the yā' and a fatḥa on the sīn, it is read by Shāmī, Ḥamza, Yazīd and Ḥafṣ; with the tā' and a fatḥa on the sīn, by Abū Bakr; with the tā' and a kasra on the sīn, by the rest.

﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا سَبَقُوا﴾ means they escaped and got away, so that they could not be overtaken. ﴿إنَّهم لا يُعْجِزُونَ﴾ means they cannot escape, and their pursuer will not find himself unable to overtake them.

(Annahum): Shāmī reads it so, meaning "because they," and each of the kasra and fatḥa readings is a causal explanation, except that the kasra reading takes the form of a fresh statement (isti'nāf), while the fatḥa reading is an explicit causal clause. Whoever reads with the tā', then "alladhīna kafarū" is the first object, and the second object is "sabaqū." Whoever reads with the yā', then "alladhīna kafarū" is the subject and "sabaqū" is the object, its underlying form being "an sabaqū," with "an" elided; "an" here is the light form of the heavy one, meaning "annahum sabaqū," and it takes the place of the two objects. Alternatively, the subject is an implied pronoun, meaning: "And let Muhammad not suppose the disbelievers to be those who escaped." As for one who claims that Ḥamza alone has this reading, there is room for scrutiny, since we have stated that he is not alone in it. It is also reported from al-Zuhrī that it was revealed concerning those who escaped from the rout of the polytheists.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 60:

﴿And prepare﴾ O believers, ﴿against them﴾ (i.e., against those who break the covenant), or against all the disbelievers, ﴿whatever you are able of power﴾, meaning of everything by which one strengthens oneself in war, including its quantity. In a hadith: "Verily, power is archery," he said it three times upon the minbar (pulpit). It was also said that power is fortresses. ﴿And of steeds kept ready﴾: this is a term for the horses that are tethered in the way of Allah. Or it is the plural of rabīṭ (a horse kept ready for war), like faṣīl and fiṣāl (young camel and its plural). Horses were singled out from among the things by which one strengthens oneself, as in His saying: ﴿and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. ﴿You will terrify thereby﴾ with what you are able of, ﴿the enemy of Allah and your enemy﴾, namely the people of Makkah. ﴿And others besides them﴾, other than them, and they are the Jews, or the hypocrites, or the people of Persia, or the disbelieving jinn. In a hadith: "Indeed, Satan does not approach the companion of a horse, nor a house in which there is a noble (ʿatīq) horse." It is also narrated that the neighing of horses terrifies the jinn.

﴿You do not know them﴾, you do not recognize them by their individual identities. ﴿Allah knows them. And whatever you spend in the way of Allah will be repaid to you in full﴾, meaning its reward will be paid to you in full.

﴿And you will not be wronged﴾ in the reward; rather, you will be given it in full.

﴿And if they incline﴾ to peace. The verb جَنَحُوا (*janahū*) means they inclined. One says جَنَحَ لَهُ and جَنَحَ إلَيْهِ, meaning he inclined toward it.

﴿to peace﴾ means to reconciliation. With the vowel *kasra* on the *sīn*, as لِلسِّلْمِ, it is the reading of Abu Bakr. The word is feminine, treated as feminine like its opposite, which is war (الحَرْبُ).

﴿then incline to it﴾ means turn toward it. ﴿And put your trust in Allah﴾, and do not fear their concealing treachery in their inclining to peace, for Allah is sufficient for you and will protect you from their plotting.

﴿Indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, who hears your words, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of your circumstances.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 62:

﴿And if they intend to deceive you﴾ — they intend to plot and to betray.

﴿Then indeed Allah is sufficient for you﴾ — Allah is sufficient for you. ﴿It is He who supported you﴾ — He strengthened you ﴿with His help and with the believers﴾ — all of them, or with the Helpers (al-Ansar).

(p-655)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 63:

﴿And He joined their hearts together﴾ — the hearts of al-Aws and al-Khazraj, after they had been enemies for a hundred and twenty years. ﴿Even if you had spent all that is in the earth, you could not have joined their hearts together﴾ — that is: their enmity had reached such a degree that if a spender had spent all the wealth that is in the earth on reconciling their relations (ṣalāḥ dhāt al-bayn, the mending of the state of affairs between them), he would not have been able to do it.

﴿But Allah joined them together﴾ — by His grace and His mercy, and He gathered their word together by His power. So He brought about between them mutual affection and love, and removed from them hatred and mutual loathing. ﴿Indeed, He is Mighty﴾ — He subdues those who deceive you. ﴿Wise﴾ — He gives victory to those who follow you.

Ya ayyuha al-Nabiyyu ḥasbuka Allahu wa-man ittaba'aka mina al-mu'minin (O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you, and so are the believers who follow you).

The wāw here carries the meaning of "with" (maʿa), and what follows it is in the accusative. The meaning is: Allah is sufficient for you, and He is sufficient for your followers among the believers as a helper. It is also permissible for it to be in the nominative position, meaning: Allah is sufficient for you, and the believers are sufficient for you.

It is said that thirty-three men and six women embraced Islam along with the Prophet ﷺ, and then ʿUmar embraced Islam, and the verse was revealed.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 65:

﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight.﴾ At-tahrid (urging): intensive encouragement to do something, from al-haras, which is when illness wears a person down until he is near death. ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a hundred of you, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve.﴾ This is a promise from Allah and good news that a group of believers, if they are steadfast, will overcome ten times their number of disbelievers, by the help and support of Allah.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ Because the disbelievers are an ignorant people who fight without seeking reward and without hoping for recompense, like beasts; so their steadfastness is weak, and they lack support because of their ignorance of Allah. This is unlike one who fights with insight, hoping for victory from Allah. It was said: it was incumbent upon them not to flee, and one would stand firm against ten; then this became burdensome for them, so it was abrogated (naskh) and lightened for them, so that one would stand against two, by His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 66:

﴿Now Allah has lightened [the burden] for you, and He knows that there is weakness in you﴾ (ḍaʿfan) is read by Ḥamzah and ʿĀṣim (with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, ḍaʿfan, rather than ḍuʿfan).

﴿So if there are among you a hundred steadfast ones﴾ is read with the yāʾ (yakun) in both places by the Kufan reader (al-Kūfī, i.e., the reader of Kufa), and al-Baṣrī (the reader of Basra, Abū ʿAmr) agreed with him in the first instance. The intended meaning of ḍaʿf here is weakness of the body.

﴿they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand by Allah's permission. And Allah is with the steadfast﴾. The repetition of the statement about a small group confronting one up to twice its number, both before and after the lightening, serves to indicate that the condition does not differ between few and many, since the situation may indeed differ between twenty confronting two hundred and a hundred confronting a thousand; and likewise between a hundred confronting two hundred and a thousand confronting two thousand.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 67:

﴿It is not for a Prophet﴾ — that is, it is not proper for him, nor is it right — ﴿that he should have captives﴾ — (read as "an yakūna" with the feminine "an takūna" variant) — ﴿until he has thoroughly subdued the land﴾. Al-ith'ān (thoroughly subduing) is the abundance of killing and exaggeration in it, derived from al-thakhāna (thickness), which means coarseness and density. It means: until he humiliates disbelief by spreading killing among its people, and exalts Islam through conquest and subjugation; then, after that, taking captives.

It was narrated: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was brought seventy captives, among them al-'Abbas, his paternal uncle, and 'Aqil. The Prophet (ﷺ) consulted Abu Bakr about them. He said: 'They are your people and your family; spare them, perhaps Allah will accept their repentance, and take ransom from them to strengthen your companions.' 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: 'They denied you and expelled you. Bring them forward and strike their necks, for these are the leaders of disbelief, and Allah has made you independent of ransom. Let 'Ali take 'Aqil, let Hamza take al-'Abbas, and let me take so-and-so, a relative of his, and we will strike their necks.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Your likeness, O Abu Bakr, is like that of Abraham when he said: ﴿Whoever disobeys me, then indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 36]. And your likeness, O 'Umar, is like that of Noah when he said: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers a single dwelling-place﴾ [Nuh: 26].'" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: "If you wish, you may kill them, and if you wish, you may take ransom from them, but a number equal to them of you will be martyred." They said: "Rather, we will take the ransom," and then they were martyred at Uhud. When they took the ransom, the verse was revealed: ﴿You desire the goods of this world﴾ — its enjoyment, meaning the ransom; he called it "'arad" (goods) because of its brief duration and swift passing away (p-657) ﴿but Allah desires the Hereafter﴾ — that is, what is the cause of Paradise, through exalting Islam by thoroughly subduing through killing. ﴿And Allah is Mighty﴾ — He overpowers the enemies — ﴿Wise﴾ — in His reproach of the close allies.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 68:

﴿Had it not been a decree from Allah﴾ — had it not been a judgment from Allah ﴿that had preceded﴾ — that He would not punish anyone for acting on ijtihad (independent reasoning, personal effort to reach a legal judgment). This was an ijtihad on their part, because they reasoned that sparing them might be a cause of their conversion to Islam, and that their ransom would strengthen them for jihad. What was hidden from them was that killing them was more honorable for Islam and more awe-inspiring to those behind them. Or [the decree refers to] what Allah had written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh), that He would not punish the people of Badr, or that He would not take them to account before clarification (al-bayan) and warning (al-i'dhar). The consultation mentioned here is evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad, and so it serves as a proof against those who reject qiyas (analogical reasoning).

"Kitab" (decree/book) is the subject (mubtada'), and "min Allah" (from Allah) is its qualifier, i.e., "Had it not been a established decree from Allah." "Sabaq" (had preceded) is another qualifier of it, and the predicate of the subject is omitted, i.e., "had it not been for a decree with this attribute existing." "Sabaq" cannot be the predicate, because the predicate of "lawla" (had it not been) never appears, ever.

﴿would have touched you﴾ — would have reached you and befallen you ﴿for what you took﴾ — from the ransom of the captives ﴿a great punishment﴾.

It is narrated: "'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found him and Abu Bakr weeping. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me; if I find something to weep over I will weep, and if I do not find it I will feign weeping.' He said: 'I weep for your companions over their taking the ransom. Their punishment was presented to me, nearer than this tree'—for a tree close to him."

It is also narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Had a punishment descended from the sky, none would have been saved from it except 'Umar and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh." This is in accordance with his saying: "Excessive slaughter in killing was more beloved to me."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 69:

﴿So eat of what you have gained﴾. It is related that they had refrained from the spoils and had not stretched out their hands toward them, so this was revealed. It has also been said that it is a permission to take ransom (fida'), because it is among the spoils. The fa' (fa) here indicates causation (al-tasbib), and the cause is omitted; its meaning is: "Indeed I have made the spoils lawful for you, so eat" ﴿lawful﴾ absolutely, "free" (mutlaqan) from reproach and punishment. It derives from "he untied the rope" (halla al-iqal), and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "what has been gained," or an adjective of the verbal noun, i.e., eating that is lawful. ﴿Good﴾, pleasant, wholesome. Or lawful by the Law (al-shar'), good by nature (al-tab'). ﴿And fear Allah﴾, so do not proceed to anything that He has not enjoined upon you in it. ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving﴾ of what you did before ﴿Merciful﴾ in making lawful what you have gained.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 70:

﴿O Prophet, say to those in your hands﴾ (i.e., in your possession), as though your hands were holding them ﴿of the captives﴾. The plural of asir (captive) is asra; Abu 'Amr reads "min al-asara" (from the captives), the plural being asra.

﴿If Allah knows any good in your hearts﴾ (i.e., sincere faith and correct intention) ﴿He will give you better than what has been taken from you﴾ (i.e., of the ransom); either He will replace it for you in this world, multiplied, or He will reward you in the Hereafter. ﴿And He will forgive you, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ It is related that: "There came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) eighty thousand from the revenue of Bahrain. He performed ablution for the noon prayer and did not pray until he had distributed it, and he ordered al-Abbas to take from it. He took from it as much as he could carry, and he would say: 'This is better than what was taken from me, and I hope for forgiveness.'" He had twenty slaves, and the least of them would trade with twenty thousand. He would say: "Allah has fulfilled one of the two promises, and I am confident of the other."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 71:

﴿And if they intend﴾ i.e., the captives, ﴿treachery against you﴾ the breaking of what they pledged to you of Islam by apostasy, or withholding what they guaranteed of ransom (fida'), ﴿then they have already betrayed God before﴾ in their disbelief in Him, and in breaking the covenant taken from every rational being concerning Him. ﴿So He gave you power over them﴾ i.e., He enabled you against them, meaning He granted you victory over them, as you saw on the Day of Badr. ﹛So He will give power over them again if they return to treachery﹜ ﴿And God is All-Knowing﴾ of the outcome ﴿All-Wise﴾ in what He commands in the present.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 72:

﴿Indeed, those who believed and emigrated﴾ from Makkah, out of love for Allah and His Messenger, ﴿and struggled with their wealth and their lives in the way of Allah﴾ — they are the Muhajirun (the emigrants). ﴿And those who gave shelter and gave help﴾ — meaning: they sheltered them in their homes and helped them against their enemies — and they are the Ansar (the helpers).

﴿They are allies of one another﴾ — meaning: some of them take charge of others in inheritance. The Muhajirun and the Ansar used to inherit from one another on account of emigration and support, to the exclusion of blood relatives, until this was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿And blood relatives are closer to one another﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. It was also said: he meant by it support and assistance. ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate﴾ from Makkah — ﴿you have no allegiance to them﴾, meaning, no inheritance from their estate. The word "walayatihim" (their allegiance) is read by Hamzah as "wilayatihim" (with a kasra on the wa); and it was said: the two readings are one and the same.

﴿Until they emigrate﴾ — so a believer who did not emigrate did not inherit from one who believed and emigrated. And since He left the name of faith for those who did not emigrate, and emigration was an obligation, so by abandoning it they became committers of a major sin, this indicates that the perpetrator of a major sin does not leave the faith. ﴿And if they seek your help﴾ — meaning: those who have embraced Islam but have not emigrated —

﴿in the matter of religion, then it is incumbent upon you to help﴾ — meaning: if fighting occurs between them and the disbelievers, and they seek assistance, then it is obligatory upon you to help them against the disbelievers. ﴿Except against a people between you and whom there is a treaty﴾ — for it is not permissible for you to help them against those (with whom you have a treaty), because they do not initiate fighting, since the treaty prevents that. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ — a warning against transgressing the limits of the Shari'ah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 73:

﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others.﴾ Its apparent meaning is the affirmation of mutual allegiance among them, but its meaning is a prohibition upon the Muslims from allying with the disbelievers, from inheriting from them, and an obligation to keep away from them and sever ties with them, even if they are relatives, and that they should not be left to inherit from one another. Then he said: ﴿Unless you do it﴾, i.e., unless you do what I have commanded you of connecting among the Muslims and befriending one another, even in inheritance, giving preference to the relationship of Islam over the relationship of kinship, and you do not make the kinship of the disbelievers as no kinship at all,

﴿there will be fitnah on earth and great corruption.﴾ There will occur fitnah on earth (p-660) and a great mischief, because as long as the Muslims do not become one hand against polytheism, polytheism will be prevalent and corruption will increase.

Qur'an 8:74: "Those who believed, emigrated, and struggled in the way of God, and those who gave shelter and helped, those are the true believers (al-mu'minun haqqan)." Because they were truthful in their faith and realized it by fulfilling its requirements: emigrating from homeland, leaving family and dwelling, and detaching from wealth and worldly life, for the sake of religion and the reward in the Hereafter. "For them is forgiveness and a generous provision" — free of any obligation (minnah), without any reproach (tankis), and without repetition (takrar), because this verse comes to praise them along with a generous promise, while the earlier verse is for enjoining mutual solidarity (al-tawasul).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 8, verse 75:

﴿And those who believed after [that] and emigrated and strove alongside you — they are of you.﴾ He means: those who came later, after the foremost (al-sabiqun) to emigrate (al-hijrah). He made them "of you" as a distinction and an encouragement. ﴿And those of kinship are nearer to one another⦆ — those related by blood are more entitled to inheritance from one another, and this is an abrogation (naskh) of inheritance by emigration and support.

﴿In the Book of Allah⦆ — in His ruling and His apportioning; or in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh); or in the Qur'an, and it is the verse of inheritance (ayat al-mawarith). It is evidence for us that the distant kindred (dhawu al-arham) inherit. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things⦆ — so He judges among His servants by whatever rulings He wills. He divided people into four categories: a category who believed and emigrated, a category who believed and gave support, a category who believed but did not emigrate, and a category who disbelieved and did not believe.
